title: State-dependent built-in references
content:
The sqlglot package maps selected SQL Server built-ins by the state they depend on. Consumers can record references or apply their own lint policy without maintaining a second list of SQL names.

Install the module with go get github.com/flanksource/sqlglot-go and import github.com/flanksource/sqlglot-go/sqlglot.

Dependency	Built-ins
environment	DB_NAME, DB_ID, SERVERPROPERTY, DATABASEPROPERTYEX, @@SERVERNAME
security	CURRENT_USER, SESSION_USER, SYSTEM_USER, USER_NAME, SUSER_SNAME, ORIGINAL_LOGIN, IS_MEMBER
session	APP_NAME, HOST_NAME, CONNECTIONPROPERTY, CONTEXT_INFO, SESSION_CONTEXT
time	GETDATE, GETUTCDATE, SYSDATETIME, SYSUTCDATETIME, SYSDATETIMEOFFSET, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
randomness	NEWID, NEWSEQUENTIALID, RAND

sqlglot.LookupBuiltin(name, dialect) looks up a SQL name without parentheses. Names are case-insensitive; the dialect accepts tsql, sqlserver, or mssql. A match returns a BuiltinFunction with its uppercase Name and typed Dependency. A false result means the name or dialect is outside this mapping; it does not establish that a function is pure. Seeded RAND remains mapped because it changes the connection's random-generator state.

expression.Builtin(dialect) identifies a mapped call or system variable in an AST node. Call it while walking a tree parsed with ParseOne or ParseScript. It recognizes anonymous calls, typed function nodes, and the double-at system-variable form. The parser preserves the original identity of calls such as GETDATE and SYSDATETIME in metadata even when both use the same AST class. Copies preserve that metadata. String literals, comments, ordinary identifiers, single-at parameters, and schema-qualified user functions do not match.

Execution-state, general metadata, and locale functions are outside this mapping. The API does not assign lint severities or execute SQL.

Run the example from this checkout:

go run ./examples/builtin-references

Expected output:

DB_NAME: environment
CURRENT_USER: security
SESSION_CONTEXT: session
GETDATE: time
NEWID: randomness

title: Command line
content:
SQL commands accept one positional SQL argument, --file, or standard input. Use --dialect (or -d) to select a dialect; neutral names the default. List the available names with sqlglot dialects.

Parse

sqlglot parse --dialect tsql 'SELECT TOP 2 name FROM users'
sqlglot parse --format json --dialect postgres 'SELECT id FROM users LIMIT 2'

The default output includes formatted SQL and the expression class. JSON output includes the reference-shaped expression tree.

For T-SQL scripts, the parser scans GO batches and reports unsupported statements with file, line, column, and a bounded SQL excerpt. It exits nonzero if any statement is unsupported. From a checkout:

sqlglot parse -d tsql --file testdata/tsql-routines/if_begin_else.sql

Validate a query

sqlglot validate --dialect postgres 'SELECT id FROM users'

validate requires one SELECT, UNION, INTERSECT, or EXCEPT query and reports its class. It does not check execution, schema names, or read-only policy. Queries can have side effects.

Format and tokenize

sqlglot format --dialect tsql 'select top 2 name from users'
printf 'SELECT id FROM users' | sqlglot tokens --format json

format changes whitespace and can handle SQL outside the parser's supported grammar. Formatting is not a parsing or validation check.

Database commands

Use sqlglot schema inspect to read a catalog or export a migration snapshot. See Set up database connections for DSNs and saved connection files, and Database inspection for a local walkthrough.

Migrate

The migration guides include separate walkthroughs for HCL schema migrations, SQL script migrations, and CSV data migrations.

Migrations work terraform-style. sqlglot migrate plan compares a desired schema or dataset with a target, writes a plan file (--out, .sqlglot-go/plan.json by default), prints a summary of what will change to stderr and the structured plan to stdout. sqlglot migrate review PLAN opens a plan file offline and prints the same summary. sqlglot migrate apply PLAN runs it: the file's own hash guards only its integrity, so there is no separate approval, and apply refuses the file with plan is stale … run sqlglot migrate plan again, running nothing, when the target changed since the plan. PostgreSQL, SQLite and CSV plans still take one --ack per destructive step.

Choose a source

Flag for plan	Contents	Target
--desired FILE	A single Atlas HCL file in the target dialect or a complete JSON snapshot from sqlglot schema inspect --snapshot	PostgreSQL and SQLite accept HCL or a matching snapshot. SQL Server requires a snapshot.
--bundle DIR	Atlas .hcl files loaded recursively as one schema declaration, plus optional .sql files	PostgreSQL, SQLite and SQL Server. Script and security support varies by target.
--csv-root DIR	CSV sources and *.csv.yaml mapping files	SQL Server reviewed data import.

Use --dsn to select the target by DSN, SQLite file path, or connection://name. --driver can override driver detection. The default target schema is public on PostgreSQL, main on SQLite and dbo on SQL Server. Use --schema to select an existing PostgreSQL schema. SQL Server HCL bundles are scoped to dbo.

To use another database as the desired schema, first export a complete snapshot from the reference, then plan against the target. The example uses two saved SQL Server connections and their default dbo schema.

sqlglot schema inspect --dsn connection://warehouse-reference --snapshot > ./desired.json
sqlglot migrate plan --dsn connection://warehouse-target --desired ./desired.json --out ./reviewed.json

Plan and apply an HCL bundle

In a new working directory, create an example SQLite database using sqlite3.

sqlite3 ./inventory-target.db 'CREATE TABLE items (id INTEGER NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL);'
mkdir ./bundle

Save this declaration as bundle/schema.hcl. It adds a nullable notes column to items.

schema "public" {}

table "items" {
  schema = schema.public

  column "id" {
    type = integer
    null = false
  }
  column "label" {
    type = text
    null = false
  }
  column "notes" {
    type = text
    null = true
  }

  primary_key {
    columns = [column.id]
  }
}

PostgreSQL and SQLite bundles use PostgreSQL-shaped HCL and declare schema "public" {}. PostgreSQL remaps that declaration when you pass --schema. SQLite projects supported HCL types and constraints onto main. With --desired, supply HCL in the target dialect and declare the target schema directly.

Bundle variables are declared with HCL variable blocks and supplied with repeatable --var 'name=HCL-literal' flags, for example --var 'label="Inventory"'. Bundles preserve omitted tables and columns by default. Pass --allow-drops when omissions should be considered for removal and review the resulting destructive changes. Treat a --desired file as the complete desired schema. Its omissions can generate drops without --allow-drops.

Plan against the existing database. The summary goes to stderr and the plan file to .sqlglot-go/plan.json; inspect it with jq.

sqlglot migrate plan --dsn ./inventory-target.db --bundle ./bundle
jq '.artifact | {hash, steps, advisory}' .sqlglot-go/plan.json

The bundle artifact is nested under artifact for PostgreSQL and SQLite, under sqlServerArtifact for a SQL Server schema-only bundle and under scriptPlan for a SQL Server bundle with scripts. A plan from --desired writes the artifact at the top level. Stdout carries the same JSON as the plan file.

After reviewing the SQL, apply the plan file. The example adds a nullable column and requires no destructive acknowledgement.

sqlglot migrate apply --dsn ./inventory-target.db .sqlglot-go/plan.json
sqlite3 ./inventory-target.db 'PRAGMA table_info(items);'

For PostgreSQL and SQLite, take acknowledgement IDs from steps entries marked destructive, and pass each complete ID once as its own --ack argument. For SQL Server, the summary shows destructive schema statements and applying the file is their acknowledgement. --lock-timeout defaults to 5s and accepts positive durations such as 30s. A schema artifact reports already-applied when its intended state is already present. If the target changed since the plan, apply fails as stale and runs nothing: plan again.

Add SQL scripts and headers

PostgreSQL and SQL Server bundles can contain SQL scripts alongside the HCL. Put directives in leading -- comment lines, before the first SQL statement or block comment. The directive names are case-sensitive.

Header	What it declares
-- phase: pre or -- phase: post	Place the script before or after schema reconciliation. The default is post.
-- dependsOn: sql/010_seed.sql, sql/020_backfill.sql	Declare these bundle-relative paths as prerequisites. A changed prerequisite makes its dependents pending, including indirect dependents. Missing paths, duplicate dependencies, cycles and dependencies from pre to post are rejected. Ready scripts in the same phase are ordered by path.
-- runs: always	Mark the script as pending every time. Rerunning an unchanged prerequisite alone leaves its declared dependents up to date.
-- transaction: true or -- transaction: false	Declare whether the script should run in a transaction. The default is true.

For a PostgreSQL preview, reuse the HCL example and save the following as bundle/010_items_view.sql.

-- phase: post
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW item_labels AS
SELECT id, label FROM items;

Save the dependent view as bundle/020_item_report.sql.

-- dependsOn: 010_items_view.sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW item_report AS
SELECT id, label FROM item_labels;

Set POSTGRES_URL to a PostgreSQL target with an existing public schema that the planner can inspect.

sqlglot migrate plan --dsn "$POSTGRES_URL" --bundle ./bundle --out ./preview.json
sqlglot migrate review ./preview.json | jq '{scripts, warnings}'

scripts reports each file's path, phase, classification (ddl, dml, mixed or unknown), parse completeness and any diagnostics. A pre script classified as ddl, mixed or unknown adds a warning because planning uses the current database state. Planning executes no script bodies and creates no migration metadata.

A PostgreSQL script bundle, or a PostgreSQL bundle with role or permission declarations, produces an advisory preview that migrate apply refuses. Schema-only bundles produce executable plans on PostgreSQL, SQLite, and SQL Server, and SQL Server bundles with scripts produce an executable script plan.

On SQL Server, use SQL Server-shaped HCL with schema "dbo" {}. For routines, pass --routines routines to treat that bundle subdirectory as declarations. Each file must be named after the routine and contain one CREATE [OR ALTER] PROCEDURE or FUNCTION batch, optionally followed by GO. The planner compares parsed definitions with the live routines. Script files outside that directory accept GO batch separators. SQLCMD directives and $(...) variables are rejected.

Plan and apply SQL Server scripts

A SQL Server bundle with scripts plans in one pass: the pre scripts, the schema statements that reconcile the declared tables and routines, then the post scripts. sqlglot derives what each script reads, writes and calls from its SQL. The summary looks like this.

Plan for sql01/inventory (scope dbo:default)

Pre-deployment scripts
  ~ re-run   pre/010_asenv.sql  source-changed

Schema (1 declared objects)
  ~ ALTER TABLE [dbo].[acme_env] ADD [label] nvarchar(20) NULL

Post-deployment scripts
  + run      post/030_seed.sql  new
  ~ re-run   post/020_report.sql  read-changed
      ~ reads SELECT Country FROM dbo.AsEnv  "ZW" → "MW"
  ! blocked  post/040_legacy.sql  reconciliation required: partial
      ? effects unknown line 3: EXEC sp_executesql @sql

Warnings
  ! script post/050_index.sql runs outside a transaction: a failure leaves it partial, blocked until reconciled

Plan: 1 to run, 2 to re-run, 1 blocked, 4 unchanged, 1 schema statements (0 destructive).

+ run is a new script, ~ re-run names why a script runs again (source-changed, script-dependency-changed, function-result-changed, read-changed, and inputs-unrecorded for a script whose version 1 content-only ledger row never recorded the inputs it now observes), ! blocked names the blocker, and ? effects unknown lists the statements whose effects could not be determined. scriptPlan.actions holds the same in JSON, and the file also records the target, the scripts with their SQL and effects, the ledger and every observed input.

A script is selected for its own source, inputs and reads as they are when the plan is made, never for what an earlier script in the plan will write; the next plan picks that up. After a script runs, apply runs each query it reads with and records the answer in the ledger. A plan runs the query again and selects the script with read-changed when the answer differs, listing the query, the recorded answer and the new one under the action's reads. A query with no recorded answer is listed but not run, and one that fails is shown with its error and selects nothing. A read that cannot run on its own, because it uses a changing variable, a temporary table or the date, or that a routine makes, is listed under untrackedReads and selects nothing.

migrate apply checks that the plan file is for the connected server and database, then re-reads the ledger and every observed input. A version 1 plan file, written before ledger scopes could be absorbed, is refused: re-run sqlglot migrate plan. Any difference fails as plan is stale: <what moved>; run sqlglot migrate plan again before anything runs. An input an upstream script writes is re-observed after that writer. After a script with unknown effects, apply re-plans; a script that is now blocked stops the apply as stale, with the scripts already committed recorded.

Review a SQL Server CSV import

Plan a CSV import with --csv-root. Review the selected files, per-table insert and update counts, and explicitDeletes and snapshotDeletes. Apply the plan file with the same CSV root and filters. For each table with deletes, pass --ack 'csv-delete:<schema.table>:<total-delete-count>:<deleteHash>' using the sum of the two reviewed delete counts and the table's deleteHash.

Run sqlglot migrate --help for the AS.csv.yaml example, including table mappings, per-file sidecars, row keys, value policies, and delete modes. The commands below use that example's country and env layers and its post-rules table.

sqlglot migrate plan --dsn connection://inventory-sqlserver --csv-root ./data \
  --layer 'country=none,ZA' --layer 'env=!dev' --csv-phase post-rules --out ./csv-review.json
sqlglot migrate review ./csv-review.json | jq '{hash, files, tables}'

For a reviewed import with zero deletes, apply with the following command.

sqlglot migrate apply --dsn connection://inventory-sqlserver --csv-root ./data \
  --layer 'country=none,ZA' --layer 'env=!dev' --csv-phase post-rules ./csv-review.json

Repeat --layer NAME=FILTER for each layer you want to override. none selects untagged files, * selects every value and !value excludes that value. The default for each layer comes from defaultFilter, which defaults to none.

--csv-phase selects tables by the phase set in YAML, which defaults to pre-rules. Omit the flag to include both phases. Apply commits pre-rules first and post-rules second. To run rule deployment between them, plan and apply each CSV phase separately. Apply revalidates the CSV sources, filters, phase, and target rows covered by the artifact.

title: Set up database connections
content:
Use --dsn to pass a database address directly, or save it once and use connection://NAME in the browser and CLI. For a comparison, save distinct connections for the desired schema and the database that receives the patch. For a file-based migration, save the target connection.

Database	DSN or path	Use with sqlglot
SQLite	./inventory.db or file:/absolute/path/inventory.db	Inspect, compare, and apply schema plans. The file must already exist.
PostgreSQL	postgres://db.example:5432/inventory?sslmode=verify-full or a PostgreSQL keyword DSN	Inspect, compare, and apply schema plans. Phased SQL bundles are advisory in the CLI.
SQL Server	sqlserver://db.example:1433?database=inventory or a SQL Server ADO/ODBC connection string	Inspect, compare, and apply schema, SQL script, and CSV plans.
MySQL and ClickHouse	A native driver DSN or URL, with --driver mysql or --driver clickhouse when needed	Inspect the catalog. The reviewed migration workflows target PostgreSQL, SQLite, and SQL Server.

For a one-off remote connection, supply the complete DSN through a shell variable, for example sqlglot schema inspect --dsn "$DATABASE_URL". Keep passwords out of examples and project files.

Save a connection in the browser

Start sqlglot ui on the machine that can reach the database and open the address it prints.

Open Connections, click Add Connection, and set the type and a name such as inventory-sqlserver.

For SQLite, select Value for Database path, enter an absolute path on the machine running sqlglot ui, and leave username and password empty. For a remote database, enter the URL for the host, database, and connection options. When username and password come from separate fields, place $(username) and $(password) in the URL where the credentials belong.

Select credential references in the username and password fields. For Kubernetes references, choose the context and namespace that contain the Secret or ConfigMap. The machine running the app needs access to that kubeconfig and permission to read those objects.

For a remote connection, click Test to check reachability. Click Add Connection to save. Run an inspection afterward to verify the database login and catalog access. SQLite is verified by inspection because there is no network endpoint to probe.

For a complete local comparison example, see Add connections and inspect a database.

Create a Connection YAML file

Save one Connection resource per .yaml, .yml, or .json file. These directories are read in order. A later directory overrides an earlier entry with the same namespace and name.

Layer	Directory
Shared	$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/flanksource/connections
sqlglot-go	$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/sqlglot-go/connections
Working directory	./.connections

The config root defaults to ~/.config when XDG_CONFIG_HOME is unset. --connections-dir DIR replaces the sqlglot-go layer for that command. The browser writes new connections to the sqlglot-go layer. Start the browser and CLI from the same working directory when they use ./.connections.

SQLite

Create the database with sqlite3 ./inventory.db 'CREATE TABLE items (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL);'. Save the resource below in .connections/inventory-local.yaml and replace the path with the file's absolute path.

apiVersion: mission-control.flanksource.com/v1
kind: Connection
metadata:
  name: inventory-local
spec:
  type: sqlite
  url:
    value: /absolute/path/to/inventory.db

PostgreSQL and SQL Server

Save this as .connections/inventory-sqlserver.yaml after replacing the host, namespace, and kubeconfig context with yours. Create or identify the Secret with the indicated username and password keys before inspecting the database.

apiVersion: mission-control.flanksource.com/v1
kind: Connection
metadata:
  name: inventory-sqlserver
  namespace: inventory
spec:
  type: sql_server
  url:
    value: 'sqlserver://$(username):$(password)@db.example:1433?database=inventory&encrypt=true'
  username:
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: inventory-db, key: username}
  password:
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: {name: inventory-db, key: password}
  properties:
    kubecontext: example-dev

For PostgreSQL, set type: postgres and use a URL such as postgres://$(username):$(password)@db.example:5432/inventory?sslmode=verify-full. Configure trusted certificates as required by the database driver.

Connection fields

Field	Meaning
apiVersion, kind	Required. Use mission-control.flanksource.com/v1 and Connection.
metadata.name	Connection name. If omitted, the name comes from the file stem.
metadata.namespace	Namespace for the connection and Kubernetes references. Use connection://NAMESPACE/NAME when referring to a namespaced connection.
spec.type	sqlite, postgres, sql_server, mysql, or clickhouse for the generic resource format shown above.
spec.url.value	Full DSN, path, or DSN template. $(username) and $(password) interpolate escaped credentials. {{.properties.KEY}} interpolates a connection property.
spec.username, spec.password	A valueFrom reference, or a value in a hand-authored resource. Each supplied field needs its placeholder in the URL. The browser saves credential references.
spec.properties	String-valued properties for the URL template. Values can be literals or references such as secret://inventory-db/host.
spec.properties.kubecontext	Kubeconfig context for this connection. Defaults to the current context when omitted.

For credential valueFrom, use one source per field. secretKeyRef: {name, key} and configMapKeyRef: {name, key} address objects in the connection namespace. helmRef: {name, key} reads a Helm release value with a JSONPath key. onePassword: 'op://vault/item/field' uses the local op CLI and its configured authentication.

Verify and reuse

sqlglot connections list
sqlglot schema inspect --dsn connection://inventory-local
sqlglot schema inspect --dsn connection://inventory/inventory-sqlserver

connections list shows each source file, layer, and any configuration warnings without resolving secrets. Inspection opens the database and reads the catalog. Use the same reference in migrate plan --dsn … and migrate apply --dsn … PLAN. For a portable project configuration, point a target alias at the saved reference.

If you see	Check
Connection missing or resolving to the wrong database	Check the working directory, config root, and layer reported by connections list. Qualify the name with its namespace.
Missing placeholder	Include $(username) or $(password) in the URL for each credential defined separately.
Missing Secret, ConfigMap, or context	Check the namespace, context, object name, key, and read access from the machine running sqlglot.
Test succeeds and inspection fails	The network endpoint is reachable. Check the database name, authentication, TLS settings, and permission to read the catalog.

title: Contributing and verification
content:
Verify the Go implementation

From the repository root:

make test
make lint
make build

The tests compare token streams, expression trees, and generated SQL with committed expectations from the pinned Python sqlglot reference. The tests do not need Python to read those expectations. make lint also requires golangci-lint v2.13.1.

make oracle regenerates expectations and generated tables and requires Python plus the reference checkout pinned in NOTICE. make oracle-exec compares actual query results using the Python execution harness and its database dependencies. Agreement with the reference alone does not prove query semantics; the execution oracle supplies a separate check.

See the repository README for coverage measurements, reference setup, and the verification model. Known reference divergences are recorded in Upstream issues.

Run the documentation site

The site uses Rspress, requires Node.js 22.12 or newer, and uses the pnpm package at the repository root. Install pnpm 12.15.0, the version pinned by package.json.

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
make docs-dev

Open the URL printed by Rspress. Markdown edits in docs/ appear automatically in the browser through live reload. Navigation lives in rspress.config.ts at the repository root. The existing docs/upstream-issues.md is served directly. Keep dependencies and generated output outside docs/ so the development server watches only documentation content.

Build and preview

make docs-check
make docs-build
make docs-preview

The check validates the TypeScript configuration. The production build checks internal links and writes the static site to doc_build/. Preview serves that output locally.

The default deployment base is /. Build for the GitHub Pages project path with pnpm docs:build --base /sqlglot-go/ and publish the contents of doc_build/ from the root of the gh-pages branch.

Render the migration diagrams

The editable Facet templates are in docs/diagrams/. Regenerate the static figures with the Facet CLI from the repository root.

mkdir -p .tmp/migration-diagrams
facet png docs/diagrams/reviewed-lifecycle.tsx docs/diagrams/selected-changes.tsx \
  --selector '#migration-diagram' --viewport 800x480 --width 1488 \
  -o .tmp/migration-diagrams
cp .tmp/migration-diagrams/reviewed-lifecycle.png .tmp/migration-diagrams/selected-changes.png docs/public/images/migrations/

title: Getting started
content:
sqlglot-go is a Go port of sqlglot. Use it as a command line tool or import its parser, generator, and migration packages into a Go application.

Install the CLI

Install the Go toolchain version declared in go.mod, then run:

go install github.com/flanksource/sqlglot-go/cmd/sqlglot@latest
sqlglot dialects
sqlglot parse --dialect tsql 'SELECT TOP 2 name FROM users'

Ensure Go's GOBIN (or GOPATH/bin when GOBIN is unset) is on your PATH. Prebuilt archives for Linux, macOS, and Windows are available on the releases page.

Build a checkout

git clone https://github.com/flanksource/sqlglot-go.git
cd sqlglot-go
make install
sqlglot parse 'SELECT id FROM users'

make install installs the current checkout into Go's binary directory. Make targets assume a POSIX shell; Windows contributors can use WSL or Git Bash.

Install the browser app from a checkout

The browser application needs a build that includes its web assets. make install builds them (Node.js and pnpm required) and embeds them, so from the checkout:

make install
sqlglot ui

A plain go install ./cmd/sqlglot leaves the web assets out, and its sqlglot ui refuses to start.

Open the address printed by sqlglot ui. This installs the browser-enabled command on your normal Go binary path; subsequent sessions start with just sqlglot ui.

Pick a workflow

Command line: parse, tokenize, format, and validate queries from an argument, file, or stdin.

Go API: parse a query and generate SQL from its expression tree.

Set up database connections: configure a target in the browser or from a YAML file, and verify it from the CLI.

Add connections and inspect a database: create and inspect two disposable SQLite databases for the comparison walkthrough.

Migrations: plan and apply changes from HCL, SQL, CSV, or a comparison between saved databases.

Contributing: run verification and work on this documentation site.

Parsing proves that the parser understands the statement. It does not establish read-only policy, validate schema names, or prove that a database will execute it.

title: Go API
content:
Install the module in an existing Go project:

go get github.com/flanksource/sqlglot-go

Parse and generate

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "github.com/flanksource/sqlglot-go/sqlglot"
)

func main() {
    tree, err := sqlglot.ParseOne("SELECT id FROM users LIMIT 2", "postgres")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    sql, err := sqlglot.Generate(tree, "postgres")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(sql)
}

ParseOne accepts one statement, including a terminating semicolon, and rejects unexpected trailing input. Generate writes the expression tree in the requested dialect and returns an error for unsupported generation. Handle both errors before executing or storing generated SQL.

The expression model exposes SQL constructs as nodes and named arguments. For the exported types and functions, see the package reference.

T-SQL scripts

sqlglot.ParseScript(source, "tsql") scans scripts and provides statement trees and diagnostics. Check the returned error, require Complete, and reject diagnostics or missing trees before relying on an analysis. Complete describes scan completion alone.

Native script analysis supports structured SQL Server routines and triggers. ParseOne retains the upstream reference's single-statement contract, which can represent some commands opaquely. Choose the entrypoint to match the analysis you need.

Formatting

sqlglot.Format(source, dialect) formats a statement; FormatScript handles scripts. These change whitespace without requiring the parser to understand every construct. Use parsing when your application needs semantic inspection.

Schema planning

The migrate and migrate/sqlserver packages compare typed schemas and generate SQL without connecting to a database. The database packages provide live inspection and migration execution. See Inspection and migrations for the boundary between planning and execution.

title: Add connections and inspect a database
content:
Save a connection once, then choose it whenever you want to inspect a database or compare its schema. This guide creates two connections, checks that they work, and shows how to return to them in your next session. See Set up database connections for DSN formats, credential references, and Connection YAML.

1. Open sqlglot

With the browser-enabled sqlglot app installed, start it:

sqlglot ui

Open the address printed in your terminal. Keep that terminal running while you use the app. The navigation contains Connections, Compare, and History.

2. Choose your databases

For a comparison, you need two connections to the same kind of database:

Connection	Purpose
inventory-reference	The database with the schema you want
inventory-target	The database you want to update

You can use existing development databases. To follow the whole guide without a database server, create the two SQLite files below instead.

Try it with SQLite

Download reference.sql and baseline.sql into a new working folder. With sqlite3 installed, run these commands in that folder:

sqlite3 inventory-reference.db '.read reference.sql'
sqlite3 inventory-target.db '.read baseline.sql'
pwd

Both databases contain an items table with two rows, Notebook and Pencil. The reference also has a notes column; the target does not. The migration guide will carry that column across without changing the rows.

Use the folder printed by pwd to form each database's absolute path, such as /Users/you/inventory-guide/inventory-reference.db. The path must be accessible to the computer running sqlglot ui. Creating a saved connection does not create the database itself.

3. Add the reference connection

Open Connections.

Click Add Connection.

Choose your database Type. For the local example, choose sqlite.

Enter inventory-reference as the Name.

For SQLite, enter the absolute path to inventory-reference.db under Database path, using the Value source. For a remote database, enter its connection URL.

For SQLite, leave username and password empty. For a remote database, select the credential references provided for that database.

For a remote database, click Test and read the result. Correct any connection or credential errors before continuing. For the local SQLite example, verify the file with the inspection command in step 5 below.

Click Add Connection to save it.

The connection now appears in the Connections list. Testing checks the current form; saving is the separate step that makes it available next time. Remote credentials are selected through references rather than saved as literal passwords. The current Test action probes network reachability and cannot test a local SQLite file; SQLite inspection actually opens and reads the file.

4. Add the target connection

Repeat Add Connection, using the name inventory-target and the target database's URL. For the local example, choose sqlite and the absolute path to inventory-target.db under Database path. Save it, then inspect both connections below.

You should now see both saved connections. Check their names and destinations before comparing them: the reference is the schema to copy from, and the target is the database to change.

5. Inspect a saved connection

You can use the same saved names from the terminal:

sqlglot connections list
sqlglot schema inspect --dsn connection://inventory-reference
sqlglot schema inspect --dsn connection://inventory-target

The inspection result lists schemas, tables, columns, and other available database objects. In the SQLite example, find items: the reference has id, label, and notes; the target has id and label.

Inspection reads the database without changing its schema. If the result says it was truncated, it is a partial catalog. The comparison workflow checks the complete supported migration schema before building a patch.

If a connection is saved in a namespace, use the namespace shown in Connections, for example connection://default/inventory-reference.

6. Reuse a saved connection

You do not need to add the connection again when you return:

Start sqlglot ui again if you stopped it.

Open Connections and find inventory-reference or inventory-target.

Click the connection to reopen its saved settings.

For a remote database, click Test to check reachability. For SQLite, run the saved connection's inspection command again.

If you changed a setting, click Save. Otherwise, close the editor and use the existing connection.

Saved connections persist across browser and application restarts on the same computer and user account. They describe how to connect; they do not keep a database session open after you stop the app. Inspection opens a connection when needed.

You can bookmark the connection's page to reopen its editor directly. If the database moved, update the saved connection and test it again rather than adding a duplicate. A connection marked read-only can be viewed and tested here, but must be edited at its source.

7. Return to an earlier inspection

Open History, choose Inspection, and click the time of the run you want to read. The saved result is available even when the original database is offline.

Opening history shows what was inspected at that time. To see the database's current schema, run sqlglot schema inspect again using the saved connection name.

Continue with a migration

Follow Compare, review, and apply a migration to choose these two saved connections, review their differences, create a patch, leave and resume the work, and apply the result.

title: CSV mapping YAML reference
content:
CSV migrations target existing SQL Server tables. Pass a directory to --csv-root. Put the optional AS.csv.yaml at its root and file-specific settings in NAME.csv.yaml beside NAME.csv. Each YAML file uses a single document with version: 1. Unknown keys, nested root configs, symbolic links, and sidecars without a corresponding CSV fail validation. Paths below are relative to the CSV root and use /.

Root config and routing

version: 1
defaults:
  schema: dbo
  tablePattern: '^(?:.*/)?(?P<table>ItemLabel)(_[A-Z]{2})?\.csv$'
  delimiter: '~'
  values:
    blank: empty-string
    nullTokens: ['\N']
    nullTokenCase: sensitive
tables:
  dbo.ItemLabel:
    key: [ID]
    phase: post-rules
  dbo.ItemStatus:
    sources: ['status.csv']
    delimiter: ','
    ignoreColumns: [SourceNote]
    delete: disabled
    values:
      columns:
        Comment:
          blank: sql-null
layers:
  country:
    values: [ZA, KE]
    match: ['**/*_${value}.csv']
    valuePattern: '[A-Z]{2}'
    defaultFilter: none
  env:
    values: [dev, qa]
    match: ['overrides/${value}/**/*.csv']
    defaultFilter: none

In this example ItemLabel.csv, ItemLabel_ZA.csv, and overrides/qa/ItemLabel_ZA.csv all route to dbo.ItemLabel. Give those files the same ID~Label header. status.csv routes to dbo.ItemStatus and uses commas.

Root field	Meaning
version	Required integer 1.
defaults	Shared file settings, plus schema and tablePattern for inferred routing.
defaults.schema	Schema for inferred tables. Defaults to the selected target schema, normally dbo.
defaults.tablePattern	Optional Go regular expression matching the entire root-relative CSV path. It must contain exactly one named capture, (?P<table>...). The captured identifier becomes the table name.
tables	Map keyed by qualified table name, such as dbo.ItemLabel. Each entry can set file options, sources, and snapshotFiles.
tables.<schema.table>.sources	List of explicit source paths or globs. ** can match nested directories. A match in more than one table is an error.
tables.<schema.table>.snapshotFiles	Exact untagged base CSV paths for delete: snapshot. Required for that mode and valid only with it. Globs are rejected.
layers	Map of named file selection layers.

Explicit sources and a sidecar table can route the same file when they agree. The regex is used when neither gives a target. Unmapped CSV paths appear in the review's unmatched list. A sidecar can omit table if the root config already routes its CSV to a table.

File settings

Defaults apply first, table settings next, then sidecar settings. The root config is optional when each file has its own sidecar. A sidecar accepts version, table, and every field in the table below. For example, labels.csv.yaml could contain:

version: 1
table: dbo.ItemLabel
key: [ID]
delimiter: ','

Setting	Default	Accepted values and behavior
key	Table primary key	An ordered list of existing key columns. Each file header must include them. Key cells must be nonempty and non-NULL. A table without a primary key requires an explicit key.
delimiter	,	A single CSV separator character, for example ~, ;, or "\t".
ignoreColumns	Empty list	Header names to ignore, matched case-insensitively. Key columns and $delete must remain usable.
phase	pre-rules	pre-rules or post-rules. All selected files for one table must agree.
delete	explicit	disabled, explicit, or snapshot. Set snapshot only on a table.
values	See below	Rules for unquoted blank and NULL values, with optional column overrides.

The CSV must be UTF-8. A UTF-8 byte-order mark is accepted. The first record is a header. Headers are trimmed and matched without case. Repeated, empty, unknown, or unwritable column names fail validation unless the column is explicitly ignored where allowed. Files for a table must share its ordered key, phase, and snapshot mode. A data row may omit a field by omitting that column from the file's header. The SQL Server target handles conversion to the destination types. Use 0x-prefixed hex for binary values, a 36-character UUID for uniqueidentifier, and 0, 1, true, or false for bit.

Value decoding

Field	Default	Meaning
values.blank	empty-string	Decode an unquoted empty field as empty-string or sql-null, or reject it with error.
values.nullTokens	['\N']	Exact tokens representing SQL NULL in unquoted fields. Use [] to clear inherited tokens. Empty strings are governed by blank.
values.nullTokenCase	sensitive	sensitive or insensitive.
values.columns.<column>	Inherited	Overrides blank, nullTokens, or nullTokenCase for one target column. Column settings cannot nest.

Quoted cells keep their text. For example, unquoted \N is SQL NULL by default, while "\N" is the literal text. "" is an empty string. Only character columns accept empty strings as values.

Layers and filters

Layer field	Meaning
values	Required nonempty list of allowed tags. none is reserved for paths without a match.
match	Required nonempty list of root-relative patterns. Each has one ${value} capture. * and ? match within one path segment, and **/ matches zero or more directory levels.
valuePattern	Optional full-match Go regular expression for tag spelling. Default [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]*.
defaultFilter	Optional selection expression for this layer. Defaults to none.

Override a filter with repeatable --layer NAME=FILTER. A file must pass every layer. A filter can include none, specific tags, or * for all tags and untagged files. Commas combine terms. !TAG excludes a tag. With only exclusions, selection starts with all values. Unknown values and conflicting tags fail planning.

For the example above, --layer 'country=none,ZA' --layer 'env=none,qa' includes the base files, the ZA files, and the QA overlays. For a shared key, the most specific row wins when its tags include all the other row's non-base tags and at least one additional tag. Identical tag sets and competing overlays without one most specific row are errors.

Delete policies and phase execution

Policy	Behavior
disabled	A $delete value of true is an error.
explicit	$delete=true deletes the exact key. Blank or false means apply the row normally.
snapshot	Deletes existing keys absent from the effective selected data. Set at table scope, declare the exact untagged snapshotFiles, and include at least one effective insert or update row.

Plan against the intended target, then review selected files, unmatched paths, row counts, and any explicitDeletes or snapshotDeletes. For each table with planned deletes, pass one --ack 'csv-delete:<schema.table>:<count>:<deleteHash>', using the sum of the two reviewed delete counts and the table's deleteHash.

--csv-phase selects one phase on both plan and apply. Without the flag, apply commits pre-rules first and post-rules second. Plan and apply each phase separately to deploy rules between them. Reuse --csv-root, all --layer filters, and --csv-phase at apply time. Changed inputs or target rows require a new plan.

For the complete plan–review–apply example, see CSV data migrations.

title: CSV data migrations
content:
Use CSV migrations to seed or reconcile rows in existing SQL Server tables. The planner reads the CSV files, YAML mappings, and current target rows and reports the changes by table.

Map a file to a table

Use a disposable SQL Server database with a saved connection named inventory-sqlserver. Set up a target table and row for the example.

CREATE TABLE dbo.ItemLabel (
    ID int NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    Label nvarchar(100) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO dbo.ItemLabel (ID, Label) VALUES (1, N'Notebook');

Save this UTF-8 file as data/labels.csv.

ID,Label
1,Hardcover notebook
2,Pencil

Save this mapping as data/labels.csv.yaml beside it.

version: 1
table: dbo.ItemLabel
key: [ID]

Each CSV header must include its match columns. Omit key to use the target table's primary key. The default delimiter is ,. By default an unquoted \N means SQL NULL. Quotes preserve literal null tokens and empty strings. Use values in YAML to define a different blank or null policy.

Review and apply

sqlglot migrate plan --dsn connection://inventory-sqlserver --csv-root ./data --out ./csv-plan.json
sqlglot migrate review ./csv-plan.json

Confirm that labels.csv routes to dbo.ItemLabel, with one insert, one update, and zero deletes. The review reports which files were selected, any unmatched paths, and each table's explicitDeletes and snapshotDeletes counts.

sqlglot migrate apply --dsn connection://inventory-sqlserver --csv-root ./data ./csv-plan.json

Apply with the same source root, layer filters, and phase used to plan. Apply revalidates the source files and relevant target rows. Verify the example with SELECT ID, Label FROM dbo.ItemLabel ORDER BY ID;. It returns 1, Hardcover notebook and 2, Pencil.

Review deletes and manage multiple files

The default delete: explicit deletes a row only when $delete is true for its key. Use delete: disabled to reject delete requests.

Table-level delete: snapshot removes target keys absent from the selected dataset. List exactly the untagged base CSVs in snapshotFiles and keep at least one effective row to insert or update. Review the resulting delete scope before applying.

For each table with deletes, pass --ack 'csv-delete:<schema.table>:<total-delete-count>:<deleteHash>', using the sum of explicitDeletes and snapshotDeletes and the reviewed table's deleteHash.

For shared mappings, place AS.csv.yaml at the CSV root. It can declare defaults, per-table sources paths or globs, and named layers. Sidecar settings override table settings, which override defaults.

For declared layers, repeat --layer NAME=FILTER to select overlays. none includes untagged files, * selects all values, and !value excludes a value. More specific tagged rows override less specific rows with the same key. Ambiguous overlays fail planning.

Set table phase to pre-rules or post-rules and pass the matching --csv-phase to plan and apply one phase. With both phases selected, apply commits each separately in that order.

The CSV mapping YAML reference covers every field and a complete AS.csv.yaml example with layer patterns and filters.

title: Supported HCL reference
content:
sqlglot uses Atlas HCL for desired schemas. The bundle format depends on the target. PostgreSQL and SQLite share a portable PostgreSQL-shaped subset. SQL Server uses its own table and column declarations.

Target	--bundle DIR	--desired FILE
PostgreSQL	Declare schema "public" {}. Use --schema to remap the declaration onto an existing schema.	Use PostgreSQL Atlas HCL declaring the target schema, or a matching inspected snapshot.
SQLite	Declare PostgreSQL-shaped schema "public" {}. sqlglot projects supported tables and types onto main.	Use native SQLite Atlas HCL declaring main, or a matching inspected snapshot.
SQL Server	Declare schema "dbo" {} with SQL Server HCL types.	Use an inspected SQL Server JSON snapshot. To supply HCL, use a bundle.

A bundle loads .hcl files recursively and evaluates them together. Cross-file references such as table.accounts.column.id are allowed. Omitted tables and columns are preserved by default. --allow-drops considers omissions on PostgreSQL and SQLite bundles. SQL Server bundles reject that switch. A --desired file represents the complete desired scope, so omissions can produce drops. Always review the resulting plan.

Variables and expressions

Declare a variable once in a bundle and reference it with var.NAME. The CLI accepts repeatable --var 'NAME=HCL_LITERAL' values. Use HCL syntax for each literal, including inner quotes for strings, for example --var 'label="Inventory"'. Defaults can be declared in HCL.

variable "label" {
  type    = string
  default = "Pending"
}

schema "public" {}

table "items" {
  schema = schema.public

  column "id" {
    type = integer
    null = false
  }

  column "label" {
    type    = text
    null    = false
    default = var.label
  }

  primary_key {
    columns = [column.id]
  }
}

sql("…") supplies a raw SQL expression where the dialect permits it. Default expressions, check expressions, and index predicates must work on the target engine. For cross-database bundles, choose expressions with the same meaning on both targets. sqlglot preserves their SQL text.

PostgreSQL

Use the PostgreSQL Atlas table syntax for columns, defaults, keys, indexes, and checks. PostgreSQL-specific attributes are available when they round-trip through the supported catalog snapshot and schema differ. An executable reviewed schema plan covers one schema and its tables. Live views, materialized views, foreign tables, partitions, row-level security, standalone sequences, routines, user triggers, domains, table inheritance, and exclusion, deferrable, or unvalidated constraints fall outside the reviewed snapshot. Use schema inspect --snapshot to check whether the catalog fits that contract.

Table block	PostgreSQL syntax
column "NAME"	type, null, and default. PostgreSQL also has identity and stored generated as blocks.
primary_key	Primary key columns, usually columns = [column.id].
unique "NAME"	Unique constraint over column references.
index "NAME"	columns or on parts, optional unique, where, include, and type, such as BTREE or GIN.
foreign_key "NAME"	columns, ref_columns, on_update, and on_delete.
check "NAME"	SQL predicate in expr.

Common column types include uuid, boolean, bytea, text, varchar(n), integer, bigint, numeric(p,s), double_precision, jsonb, date, and timestamptz(p). The Atlas references define the complete PostgreSQL syntax. Check availability against sqlglot's bundled Atlas version and reviewed table scope before using newer features. Atlas PostgreSQL HCL reference · Atlas type syntax · Bundled PostgreSQL type registry

Roles and permissions

PostgreSQL bundles can declare roles and permissions for advisory review. A bundle containing either generates an advisory plan that migrate apply refuses.

Block or field	Accepted form
role "NAME"	One role name. Boolean attributes are external, login, inherit, superuser, create_db, create_role, replication, and bypass_rls. inherit defaults to true; the others default to false.
role.conn_limit	Integer connection limit, default -1.
role.comment	Optional string.
role.member_of	List of role references, for example [role.inventory_readers].
permission.to	Required grantee, such as role.inventory_reader or PUBLIC.
permission.for	Required schema, table, column, or sequence reference.
permission.privileges	Required nonempty privilege list. Use a privilege valid for the target or ALL.
permission.grantable	Optional boolean, default false.
permission.for_each	Optional collection. Use each.value in the permission body to expand one grant per entry.

Permission target	Privileges
Schema	USAGE, CREATE
Table	SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, MAINTAIN
Column	SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, REFERENCES
Sequence	USAGE, SELECT, UPDATE

Portable bundles for SQLite

Use one schema "public" {} and at least one table. SQLite accepts the following PostgreSQL-shaped declarations in a bundle.

Block	Supported form
variable	Values and defaults evaluated before projection.
table "NAME"	Declare schema = schema.public. Supported table attributes are named checks.
column "NAME"	type, null, and a literal or sql(...) default.
primary_key	Column references.
unique "NAME"	Column references. Becomes a named unique index in SQLite.
index "NAME"	Column references, optional unique and where, and default or explicit B-tree method.
foreign_key "NAME"	columns, ref_columns, on_update, and on_delete. Actions include NO_ACTION, RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET_NULL, and SET_DEFAULT.
check "NAME"	expr, preserved as SQL.

PostgreSQL HCL family	SQLite projection
uuid	text without UUID-format enforcement
text, char, character, varchar, character_varying, bpchar, name	text, without length enforcement
json, jsonb	text with a json_valid check named <table>_<column>_json
date, time, timetz, timestamp, timestamptz	datetime, without precision or timezone enforcement
int2, int4, int8, int, integer, smallint, bigint, xid, xid8	integer
bool, boolean	bool with SQLite numeric affinity
bytea	blob
numeric, decimal	numeric, without precision or scale enforcement
real, float, float4, float8, double_precision	real

SQL spellings containing spaces can use sql(), for example sql("timestamp with time zone") or sql("character varying(100)"). SQLite rejects other type families, including arrays, enums, domains, ranges, serial types, and user-defined types. It also rejects generated and identity columns, expression indexes, per-index-column attributes, foreign-key attributes beyond the portable fields, triggers, schema objects such as views, role and permission blocks, and bundled .sql scripts. A check with a generated JSON-check name must use the matching JSON validation expression.

The projection rules above apply to --bundle. With --desired, use the native SQLite table syntax for schema "main" {} and ensure the plan can round-trip the target catalog. Atlas SQLite HCL reference

SQL Server bundles

Declare one schema "dbo" {}. SQL Server schema bundles manage declared tables and routines in dbo. Omitted tables, columns, routines, and extra indexes are preserved. Review any planned constraint changes.

Block	Supported form
table "NAME"	schema = schema.dbo, with columns, keys, indexes, foreign keys, and checks.
column "NAME"	type, null, default, and optional identity { seed, increment }. Both identity attributes are integers. Defaults can use a literal or sql("getdate()").
primary_key	Column references, optional name, and clustered. The key is clustered by default.
index "NAME"	columns or column on parts with optional desc, plus unique, clustered, include = [column.x], and where. Indexes default to nonclustered.
foreign_key "NAME"	columns, ref_columns, on_delete, and on_update. Use SQL Server's supported actions NO_ACTION, CASCADE, SET_NULL, and SET_DEFAULT.
check "NAME"	expr.

Family	Types
Integers and bit	bit, tinyint, smallint, int, bigint
Exact numeric	decimal(p,s), numeric(p,s), money, smallmoney
Approximate numeric	real, float(n)
Character	char(n), varchar(n), nchar(n), nvarchar(n), text, ntext
Binary	binary(n), varbinary(n), image, rowversion
Temporal	date, time(p), datetime, datetime2(p), smalldatetime, datetimeoffset(p)
Other	uniqueidentifier, xml, sql_variant

Use sql("nvarchar(max)"), sql("varchar(max)"), or sql("varbinary(max)") for (max). sql("timestamp") is an alias for rowversion. float precision up to 24 bits uses real storage.

SQL Server rejects computed columns, user-defined and alias types such as sysname, and unsupported table or column attributes. It also rejects declared tables with unsupported partitioning or triggers and changes to an existing column's identity. HCL blocks for views, triggers, sequences, functions, and procedures are not supported. Use --routines DIR for one CREATE [OR ALTER] PROCEDURE or FUNCTION batch per .sql file named after the routine. Use SQL deployment scripts for ordered executable statements, such as creating a view.

For a runnable schema migration, see HCL schema migrations.

title: HCL schema migrations
content:
Use Atlas HCL to describe the schema you want. migrate plan compares the declaration with the target catalog and generates SQL to reconcile the differences.

See the supported HCL reference for blocks, types, and restrictions by target.

Choose the input

Input	Scope and target
--bundle DIR	Loads .hcl files recursively as one declaration. Omitted tables and columns are preserved by default. Use --allow-drops to consider omissions for removal.
--desired FILE	Treats one file as the complete desired scope. Omissions can generate drops. PostgreSQL and SQLite accept HCL in the target dialect or a matching JSON snapshot. SQL Server requires a snapshot for this flag.

For a bundle, declare schema "public" {} on PostgreSQL and SQLite. PostgreSQL can remap it to an existing schema selected with --schema. SQLite projects supported types and constraints onto main. SQL Server bundles use SQL Server HCL types and declare schema "dbo" {}. For a single HCL file passed to --desired, declare the target schema directly.

Add a column in SQLite

From a new directory, create a disposable database, a table, and a row.

sqlite3 ./inventory.db "CREATE TABLE items (id INTEGER NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); INSERT INTO items VALUES (1, 'Notebook');"
mkdir ./schema

Save this as schema/items.hcl.

schema "public" {}

table "items" {
  schema = schema.public

  column "id" {
    type = integer
    null = false
  }
  column "label" {
    type = text
    null = false
  }
  column "notes" {
    type = text
    null = true
  }

  primary_key {
    columns = [column.id]
  }
}

Plan the bundle and review the saved file.

sqlglot migrate plan --dsn ./inventory.db --bundle ./schema --out ./schema-plan.json
sqlglot migrate review ./schema-plan.json

Check that the plan adds the nullable notes column and contains zero destructive steps. For a PostgreSQL or SQLite plan with destructive steps, find the steps entries marked destructive and pass each full ID as a separate --ack argument. Review SQL Server schema statements in the plan summary before applying, including any destructive ones.

sqlglot migrate apply --dsn ./inventory.db ./schema-plan.json
sqlite3 ./inventory.db 'SELECT id, label, notes FROM items ORDER BY id;'

The query returns 1|Notebook|. The existing row remains and its new notes value is NULL.

Extend the bundle

Pass values for HCL variable blocks using repeatable --var 'NAME=HCL_LITERAL' arguments, such as --var 'label="Inventory"'.

On SQL Server, pass --routines routines to load declarative routine definitions from that subdirectory. Use one procedure or function per file and name each file after its routine. The planner compares the parsed definition with the live database.

Keep deployment SQL alongside the declarations when you need phased scripts. PostgreSQL script bundles and PostgreSQL bundles that declare roles or permissions produce advisory previews. See SQL script migrations for deployment order and executable targets.

title: Migrations
content:
Start with the source that describes what you want to change. HCL reconciles a declared schema, SQL runs deployment scripts, and CSV reconciles rows in existing tables.

Source	Use it for	Targets
HCL schema migrations	Declare tables, columns, and constraints and generate the SQL to reconcile them	PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server
SQL script migrations	Version deployment scripts, order dependencies, and review what will run	SQL Server apply, PostgreSQL advisory preview
CSV data migrations	Preview inserts, updates, and deletes from CSV and YAML mappings	SQL Server
Compare two databases	Inspect two saved connections and turn selected schema differences into a patch	PostgreSQL, SQLite, SQL Server

Plan, review, and apply

Inspect. Identify the target and the scope you intend to change. Use a DSN, a SQLite file path, or a saved connection.

Plan. Run sqlglot migrate plan with the source and target. Planning reads the target, prints a summary, and writes .sqlglot-go/plan.json by default. Use --out to choose a different path.

Review. Run sqlglot migrate review PLAN to inspect the saved file offline. Check the target, warnings, SQL or row counts, and any destructive changes. Keep the reviewed file intact so its integrity hash remains valid.

Apply. Run sqlglot migrate apply --dsn TARGET PLAN. Apply rechecks the target against the plan before executing it. If it reports a stale plan, plan again and review the new file. CSV plans also need the original source root, filters, and phase at apply time.

For PostgreSQL, SQLite, and CSV plans, pass one --ack per destructive item that you reviewed. The source guides explain how to find the required identifiers. After applying, inspect the resulting schema or data before proceeding.

Configuration reference

Project YAML for target aliases, source selection, labels, and CEL transforms.

CSV mapping YAML for tables, keys, layers, and delete modes.

Supported HCL for dialect-specific blocks, types, and restrictions.

SQL script headers for phases, dependencies, reruns, and transactions.

title: Project YAML reference
content:
Place .sqlglot-go.yaml in a migration project. Use it to select HCL and SQL sources and give your database targets stable names. Use CSV mapping YAML for CSV imports.

Complete example

version: 1
connections:
  dev: 'connection://inventory/inventory-sqlserver'
  local: './inventory.db'
mappings:
  - match: 'schema/**/*.hcl'
  - match: 'scripts/**/*.sql'
    labels:
      component: [inventory]
  - match: 'descriptors/**/*.xml'
    kind: sql
    transform: >-
      {"sql": read(xmlpath(file.content, "/migration/@script")),
       "id": xmlpath(file.content, "/migration/@id").trim().lower(),
       "phase": "post"}
ignore:
  - 'scripts/archive/**'

The descriptor rule reads a file such as descriptors/labels.xml containing <migration id="seed-labels" script="labels.sql"/>. Keep labels.sql beside the XML file and outside the direct scripts/**/*.sql match. Its ledger ID is seed-labels. dev uses a saved SQL Server connection; local is an example alias for projects with SQLite-compatible sources.

sqlglot migrate plan --target dev --out ./reviewed.json
sqlglot migrate review ./reviewed.json
sqlglot migrate apply --target dev ./reviewed.json

Root fields

Field	Type	Rule
version	Integer	Required. Must be 1.
connections	Map of alias to string	Each value is a nonempty DSN, SQLite .db path, or connection:// reference. Alias names start with an ASCII letter or digit and may continue with letters, digits, _, ., or -.
mappings	List of mapping rules	Selects the HCL and SQL sources. With mappings configured, only matched files enter the bundle.
ignore	List of globs	Excludes matching files and directories, including companion files read by transforms.

Use one YAML document. Unknown keys fail validation. At least one mapping or connection is required. --target is mutually exclusive with --dsn. Relative SQLite .db paths in an alias are resolved beside this YAML file. connection:// aliases use the normal saved connection layers.

Without a source argument, migrate plan searches the working directory first and the Git root second. migrate plan DIR and migrate plan --bundle DIR look for the file in DIR. An explicit --desired or --csv-root selects its own source, and can use --target for the database.

Mapping fields

Field	Type	Rule
match	Glob	Required. Match a case-sensitive, project-relative path using /; ** spans directories.
kind	hcl or sql	Optional. Defaults to the .hcl or .sql extension, or to the transform result for another extension.
labels	Map of name to string list	Optional metadata shown in the structured plan and script review. Label names and list entries must be nonempty.
transform	CEL expression	Optional source conversion and metadata projection. It receives file.path and file.content.

Hidden files and directories are skipped during discovery. A file can match at most one mapping, and every selected source needs a unique ID and bundle path. By default the ID is the matched path normalized to the source extension. Planning fails if configured mappings select no sources.

Transform result

Return a map with exactly one content field, sql or hcl. Its kind must agree with any explicit or inferred kind.

Key	Type	Rule
sql	String	SQL text to plan.
hcl	String	HCL declaration to plan.
id	String	Optional stable source ID. For HCL it must be a project-relative .hcl path. For SQL it is the ledger ID and the name other scripts use in dependsOn.
name	String	Optional SQL display name. Defaults to the ID and determines the order of ready scripts within a phase.
phase	pre or post	Optional SQL phase. If the SQL also declares -- phase:, the two values must agree.
labels	Map of name to string list	Overrides individual mapping labels. An empty list removes the label.

read(path) reads a regular file relative to the matched source's directory. Use a relative path within the project. If that companion matches an ignore rule, the mapping is skipped. xmlpath(xml, selector) returns the text or attribute value from exactly one XPath match. Zero or multiple matches fail the plan.

title: SQL script headers reference
content:
These directives apply to SQL migration scripts selected through a bundle, positional source paths, or project YAML. SQL Server can apply script plans. PostgreSQL can preview them as advisory plans. SQL Server declarative routine files selected by --routines are handled separately from deployment scripts.

Header syntax

Put directives in leading -- line comments. Blank lines and ordinary -- comments are allowed. The first nonblank line that is not a -- comment ends the header, including a /* … */ comment. Names and values are case-sensitive. Write the colon immediately after the directive name, as shown below. Other line comments are treated as comments, so check the resulting phase and policy in the plan if you suspect a typo.

-- Apply this view after the referenced view is available.
-- phase: post
-- dependsOn: sql/010_item_labels.sql
-- transaction: true
CREATE OR ALTER VIEW dbo.item_report AS
SELECT ID, Label FROM dbo.item_labels;
GO

Header	Accepted values	Default and effect
-- phase:	pre, post	post. Pre scripts run before the schema reconcile, then post scripts run after it. A mapped phase must agree with an explicit header.
-- dependsOn:	Comma-separated script IDs	No explicit dependencies by default. For ordinary bundles, IDs are bundle-relative SQL file paths. For mapped SQL, use the assigned ID.
-- runs:	always	Omit the header for normal change-based selection. always makes an otherwise eligible script pending every time.
-- transaction:	true, false	true. All batches in a transactional SQL Server script run in one transaction. A failure with false can leave partial effects that require reconciliation.

Dependency ordering and reruns

For dependsOn, write full IDs from the bundle root, even when two files share a subdirectory. Whitespace around entries is ignored. Missing IDs, duplicate dependencies, cycles, and a pre script depending on a post script are errors. Among ready scripts in the same phase, order is by name and then ID. Ordinary scripts use their paths for both. Mapped scripts can set a name in the transform result.

A changed declared prerequisite can make its dependents pending, including indirect dependents. An unchanged prerequisite selected only by runs: always does not make its dependents pending for that reason alone. SQL Server can also rerun a script when an observed read or function result changed since its last successful run. Explicit dependsOn entries set ordering even where an effect cannot be inferred from the SQL.

The planner uses the current database without running the script bodies. Changes made by apply can select additional readers on the next plan. Review scriptPlan.actions or the CLI summary for + run, ~ re-run, ! blocked, and ? effects unknown. Inspect warnings before applying. After a script with unknown effects, SQL Server rechecks the plan and can stop if a later action becomes blocked.

SQL Server batches

Use a standalone GO line between batches. A GO inside a comment or string does not split the script. GO repeat counts, batch separators combined with SQL on the same line, SQLCMD directives such as :setvar and :r, and $(...) scripting variables are rejected. Resolve those directives or variables before planning. A script with no executable statements is skipped and reported in the plan.

For a working pair of dependent scripts and the plan commands, see SQL script migrations.

title: SQL script migrations
content:
Use SQL scripts for changes you want to express as executable statements, such as adding a view or backfilling data. SQL Server supports executable script plans. PostgreSQL script bundles produce advisory previews. SQLite supports schema migrations through HCL.

Create a script bundle

Use a disposable SQL Server target with an existing dbo.ItemLabel table containing ID and Label columns. See saved connections to register it as inventory-sqlserver. Keep the database preparation separate from the migration bundle. For example, run the following once on an empty test database.

CREATE TABLE dbo.ItemLabel (
    ID int NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    Label nvarchar(100) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO dbo.ItemLabel (ID, Label) VALUES (1, N'Notebook');

Save the first script as db/010_item_labels.sql.

-- phase: post
CREATE OR ALTER VIEW dbo.item_labels AS
SELECT ID, Label FROM dbo.ItemLabel;
GO

Save the second script as db/020_item_report.sql.

-- dependsOn: 010_item_labels.sql
CREATE OR ALTER VIEW dbo.item_report AS
SELECT ID, Label FROM dbo.item_labels;
GO

The paths in a dependency header are relative to the bundle directory. SQL Server accepts GO batch separators. Resolve SQLCMD commands and $(...) references before passing the script to sqlglot.

Set order and execution policy

Put case-sensitive directives in leading -- comments before the first SQL statement or block comment.

Directive	Behavior
-- phase: pre or -- phase: post	Run before or after schema reconciliation. The default is post.
-- dependsOn: 010_first.sql, 020_second.sql	Order scripts by their prerequisites. Changes to a prerequisite can make its transitive dependents pending. A pre script cannot depend on a post script. Ready scripts in the same phase are ordered by path.
-- runs: always	Select this script every time. An unchanged prerequisite selected by this rule alone leaves its dependents up to date.
-- transaction: true or -- transaction: false	Run transactionally by default. A failure outside a transaction can leave partial effects that require reconciliation.

An HCL bundle can include scripts. Apply runs selected pre scripts, reconciles the declared schema, then runs selected post scripts. See the SQL script headers reference for ordering, batch syntax, and accepted values. Use project YAML for source mappings and connection aliases.

Plan, review, and apply

sqlglot migrate plan --dsn connection://inventory-sqlserver --bundle ./db --out ./script-plan.json
sqlglot migrate review ./script-plan.json

For the example, confirm both scripts are new and that 010_item_labels.sql comes before 020_item_report.sql. In a SQL Server plan, look for these statuses in the summary or scriptPlan.actions in JSON.

Status	What to review
+ run	A new script and its SQL.
~ re-run	The reason, such as changed source, an explicit dependency, or a recorded query whose result changed. For a tracked read, review both recorded and current results.
! blocked	An item requiring attention, such as a partially applied script. Reconcile it and plan again before proceeding.
? effects unknown	Statements whose effects the planner could not determine, such as some dynamic SQL. Review those statements directly.

Planning reads the current target and executes no script bodies. A row or routine result changed by a script during apply can cause its readers to be selected on the next plan. Apply checks the ledger and observed inputs before running and refuses a stale plan.

sqlglot migrate apply --dsn connection://inventory-sqlserver ./script-plan.json

Verify the two views by running SELECT ID, Label FROM dbo.item_report; on the target. For the disposable example, it returns 1, Notebook.

title: Compare, review, and apply a migration
content:
This guide follows one complete migration: choose two saved connections, inspect the differences, create a patch, leave and resume the review, then apply it to the target. Start with Add connections and inspect a database if you have not saved your connections yet. For file-based migrations, see the migration guides.

The example uses inventory-reference and inventory-target. The reference's items table has a notes column that the target is missing. Both databases already contain two rows.

1. Choose the saved connections

Start the app if it is not already running:

sqlglot ui

Open Compare.

Under Reference (desired), select inventory-reference.

Under Target (to patch), select inventory-target.

Leave the optional Schemas field empty for this example.

Click Compare.

You can use New connection beside either picker if a connection has not been added yet. The two connections must point to distinct databases of the same kind. Check the direction before continuing: the reference supplies the desired schema, and the target receives the changes.

2. Read the differences

The review opens with the connection names and counts of added, changed, and dropped objects.

In Changes, open the items table.

Read its Diff to see what is present in the reference and missing from the target.

Open Migration SQL to read the SQL for the selected changes.

Check the box for adding notes.

For the SQLite example, the SQL adds one nullable column:

ALTER TABLE `items` ADD COLUMN `notes` text NULL

Review the checked changes even if they were selected automatically. Leave changes you do not want unchecked. Destructive changes are identified in the review; they require explicit acknowledgement before apply.

3. Create the patch

Click Create patch (1) for the example's single selected change. If the selection needs another change, use Add required changes, review the expanded selection, and then create the patch.

The patch screen shows:

Patch — the number of selected changes and the plan file's hash.

SQL script — the statements the patch will execute.

Apply to the target — the command for applying this plan file to the selected target.

Read the SQL and confirm the target connection. Click plan.json to download the plan file. You can also download patch.sql for a readable copy of the SQL. Keep the plan file unchanged after reviewing it: its hash guards its integrity, so an edited file is refused.

Creating the patch checks the databases again. If their schemas changed since the comparison, use Re-compare and review the new differences before making another patch.

4. Leave and resume the work

You can close the browser and return later. If you also stopped sqlglot, run sqlglot ui again on the same computer and user account.

Reopen a comparison

Open History.

Choose Comparison and, if helpful, select inventory-target in the Connection filter.

Find the run by its connection names and time.

Click its time to reopen the comparison review.

You can inspect its saved differences and choose changes without contacting either database. The notice at the top says the comparison was recorded. Creating a new patch contacts the databases and checks whether that comparison is still current.

If you want to preserve your exact selection and focused object, bookmark the review page before leaving. The page address retains those choices. Opening a comparison from History restores the comparison and starts with its default selection, so review the checked changes again.

Reopen a patch

In History, choose Patch.

Open the patch by its time.

Review the saved SQL, download plan.json again if needed, or copy the same apply command.

Reopening a patch does not regenerate or apply it. Its saved contents remain available if a database is offline. You can also bookmark the patch page to return directly to it.

Get a fresh comparison

Click Re-compare when you need the latest schema state. It runs a new comparison and keeps the earlier run in History. A saved comparison is a record of the past, not a live view of the database.

5. Apply the reviewed patch

The browser prepares and downloads the patch; execution happens in the terminal.

Put the downloaded plan.json in your working folder.

In Apply to the target, click Copy command.

Open a terminal in that folder.

Read the command and confirm that its connection is inventory-target.

Run the copied command.

The command has the form sqlglot migrate apply --dsn <target> [--ack <id>…] plan.json: the saved target connection, any required destructive acknowledgements, and the plan file as its last argument. You do not need to assemble these values manually, and there is no hash to pass: apply checks the file's own hash and refuses the plan, running nothing, if the target changed since it was planned. Review destructive changes before running a command that acknowledges them.

A successful apply reports applied. For the SQLite example, one step adds notes and the two existing rows remain. You can check them from the folder containing the database:

sqlite3 inventory-target.db 'SELECT id, label, notes FROM items ORDER BY id;'

Expected result:

1|Notebook|
2|Pencil|

6. Verify and return later

Open the saved comparison again and click Re-compare. After applying the example's only change, the review says the two connections have identical schemas and there is nothing to patch.

If you selected only some changes from a larger comparison, the unselected differences should still appear. Review those separately when you are ready.

Open History and choose Migration to read the apply result. The original comparison and patch are still available as records of what you reviewed. Restarting the app does not remove saved connections or completed runs.

Running the same schema plan file again reports already-applied when the target already matches its expected result. If apply reports drift or a stale plan, return to Compare, run a fresh comparison, and review a new patch instead of editing the old plan file.

Plan and apply from the terminal

The CLI works the same way terraform does: plan writes a file, apply runs exactly that file.

sqlglot migrate plan --dsn connection://inventory-target --bundle ./db
sqlglot migrate review .sqlglot-go/plan.json
sqlglot migrate apply --dsn connection://inventory-target .sqlglot-go/plan.json

plan prints what will change to stderr, terraform-style: + run for new scripts, ~ re-run with the reason (for example read-changed, with the query and its answer then and now), ! blocked, ? effects unknown, the schema statements with destructive ones marked, warnings and totals. The plan file's hash only guards its integrity; there is nothing else to approve. If the database changed after the plan, apply stops with plan is stale: <what moved>; run sqlglot migrate plan again and runs nothing. See the CLI guide for every source and flag.

If something goes wrong

What you see	What to do
A saved connection no longer works	Open it in Connections, test it, correct its settings or credential reference, and save
No connections in a picker	Add and save a connection first; fix any warnings shown in Connections
Identical schemas	There is no change to apply; check that you selected the intended pair
Missing required changes	Add the required changes, then review the selection and SQL again
A database changed since review	Re-compare and create a newly reviewed patch
The plan file is refused as invalid	Download plan.json again from the same saved patch as the copied apply command; do not edit it
A database is offline	Read the saved comparison or patch in History; reconnect before creating or applying a new patch
The commit result is unknown	Inspect the target and its migration history before deciding whether to retry

To inspect a saved database directly from the terminal at any time, use sqlglot schema inspect --dsn connection://inventory-target.
